q: Growers across southern Italy plant high on the Apennine slopes. What does the elevation chiefly buy them?
opts: Cooler nights that preserve acidity and aroma
exp: A wide day-to-night swing slows sugar accumulation relative to flavour development. In a hot climate that is the main tool for keeping freshness in the glass.

q: A label reads DOCG. What does that final letter add over a DOC wine?
opts: A guarantee of at least ten years of ageing
A guarantee backed by chemical analysis and a tasting panel
A guarantee that the fruit was farmed organically
exp: DOC wines face laboratory and tasting examination too, so Garantita is a matter of degree: the panel tastes lot by lot at bottling and every bottle carries a numbered state seal, the contrassegno. The production rules behind a DOCG, yields and ageing among them, are stricter as well.

q: Under EU classification, DOC and DOCG wines are grouped together as what?
exp: DOP covers every protected designation of origin, and IGT wines fall into the broader IGP band. The older Italian initials still appear on most labels.

q: Which term on an Italian label marks the historic heart of a denomination?
exp: Classico zones are the original delimited areas, later ringed by expansions of the same name. Chianti Classico and Soave Classico are the familiar examples.

q: A producer holds a wine well past the standard minimum to earn one extra word on the label. Which word?
exp: National law sets the floor at two years of ageing for reds and one year for whites, and an individual denomination's rules may demand longer still. Riserva frequently carries a higher minimum alcohol as well.

q: A denomination allows one extra word for wines meeting a higher minimum alcohol. Which word is it?
exp: Superiore usually pairs the alcohol requirement with lower permitted yields. It says nothing about oak, vineyard site or a tasting assessment.

q: Tuscan reds blending Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon fell outside the DOC rules entirely. Which category was created in 1992 to house them?
exp: Before 1992 those wines were sold as plain table wine despite their price. IGT gave them a legitimate geographic designation, and many Super Tuscans still choose Toscana IGT.

q: Barolo and Barbaresco are both built on which single grape?
exp: Both denominations require one hundred percent Nebbiolo, so what separates them is site, soil and ageing rather than variety. The grape gives pale colour with fierce tannin and acidity.

q: Which grape supplies Piedmont's high-acid, low-tannin everyday red around Asti and Alba?
exp: Barbera is the region's most planted red. It ripens with striking acidity and very little tannin, which is why it drinks young and sits so well against food.

q: A deeply coloured, low-acid Piedmontese red ripens weeks ahead of Nebbiolo. Which grape is it?
exp: Dolcetto's early ripening lets growers use the cooler sites where Nebbiolo would never finish. The name means little sweet one and refers to the fruit, not the wine, which is dry.

q: Roero's white DOCG rests on a grape that was close to extinction in the 1970s. Name it.
exp: Arneis was revived in the Roero hills across the Tanaro from the Langhe. It is rounder and less acidic than Cortese, with a pear and almond character.

q: Two Nebbiolo denominations in the far north of Piedmont call the grape Spanna. Which pair?
exp: Alto Piemonte sits well north of the Langhe on volcanic and glacial soils. Its Nebbiolo is lighter framed and often blended with small amounts of local varieties.

q: Between Barolo and Barbaresco, which carries the longer minimum ageing before release?
exp: Barolo needs longer in total and longer in wood than Barbaresco, and both extend further again for Riserva. Barbaresco's fruit ripens slightly earlier, which suits the shorter requirement.

q: A gently sparkling, sweet, low-alcohol Piedmontese wine is pressed from Moscato Bianco. Which is it?
exp: Fermentation is stopped early, leaving sugar, grape aroma and around five and a half percent alcohol. The wine is frizzante rather than fully sparkling.

q: Lombardy's traditional-method sparkling DOCG takes its name from a zone near Brescia. Which is it?
exp: Franciacorta uses Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco with the second fermentation in bottle. It is the Italian benchmark for that style and is priced accordingly.

q: Steep terraces above the Adda valley in Lombardy grow Nebbiolo under a local name. What is it called there?
exp: Valtellina's terraces are among the steepest worked vineyards in Italy, all of it hand labour. Sforzato is the zone's dried-grape version of the same grape.
